newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council told of Sudan charge against Ethiopia.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council told of Sudan charge against Ethiopia.

text.p: The Security Council discussed a Sudanese allegation of aggression by Ethiopia during closed-door consultations on Wednesday but took no immediate action pending further information.
"I reported to the informal consultations the question of Sudan in connection with the visit of the ambassador of Sudan who came to see me," council President Hisashi Owada of Japan told reporters.

During that meeting on Tuesday, Sudanese U.N. envoy Elfatih Erwa "explained the situation on the border area and requested that the Security Council take appropriate measures regarding the matter," Owada said.

Council members made a few comments during the consultations, "but for the moment it was felt that there was not sufficient information as to exactly what was taking place ... and we decided to keep ourselves informed on the developments for the moment," he added.
In a letter to Owada circulated on Wednesday, Sudanese Foreign Minister Ali Osman Mohamed Taha listed a number of alleged "acts of provocation and aggression" by Ethiopia.
He said they included shelling by heavy artillery on Jan. 12 "resulting in the destruction of the town of Kurmuk, capital of the governorate of Kurmuk in the Blue Nile State."

Taha said this followed an attack by an Ethiopioan infantry division comprising 6,000 men supported by 22 tanks, "accompanied by a few elements of the rebel movement, the so-called Sudanese People's Liberation Army (SPLA) under the command of Ethiopian officers."

He said the areas "attacked and overrun by the Ethiopian army" were exactly on the border between the two countries and that the only access was across the border and from Ethiopian military camps established there.

Taha said the "Ethiopian aggression" was a flagrant violation of the U.N. Charter, international norms and the principles of good neighbourliness and also "represents a serious threat to international peace and security."

Reserving his country's right of self-defence, he called on the Security Council to "take whatever measures are necessary to secure the respect by Ethiopia for the letter and spirit" of the U.N. Charter, to compel it to withdraw its forces from Sudanese territory and to refrain from any repetition.
